choices.text: Because the bars are the wrong colour
Because the unit boxes are not all the same length, so the bars are not to scale
Because bar models must always use 7 units

questions.feedback: That trap answer is the one to unlearn: Drawing unit boxes in any lengths, guessing the sizes. Reteach point: Every unit box must be exactly the same length: two units is exactly twice one unit. Check every unit box against the first one before you trust the lengths in a model.
questions.misconception: Drawing unit boxes in any lengths, guessing the sizes.
questions.prompt: A pupil draws the unit boxes of a bar model in any lengths, guessing the sizes, so the 2-unit bar is only a little longer than the 1-unit bar. Why can this model not be trusted?

questions.feedback: Scene s1 fixes the method: count the equal unit boxes in both bars - 2 for Mia and 3 for Ben - giving 5 units altogether.
questions.prompt: Mia has 2 units and Ben has 3 units, drawn with equal unit boxes. How many units do Mia and Ben have altogether?

questions.feedback: Scene s2 fixes the reading: one unit moves away from the before bar, so the after bar has 3 - 1 = 2 units.
questions.prompt: Mia has 3 units and gives 1 unit away. Her before bar has 3 units. How many units does her after bar have?

questions.feedback: Scene s3 fixes the method: compare the two parts of the part-whole bar and subtract, diff = 4 - 3 = 1 unit.
questions.prompt: A whole bar has 7 units. 3 units are boys and 4 units are girls. What is the difference between the girls' units and the boys' units?
